title: PATIENT-PSI: Using Large Language Models to Simulate Patients for Training Mental Health Professionals

paper.authors: Ruiyi Wang, Stephanie Milani, Jamie C. Chiu, Jiayin Zhi, Shaun M. Eack, Travis Labrum, Samuel M. Murphy, Nev Jones, Kate Hardy, Hong Shen, Fei Fang, Zhiyu Zoey Chen
paper.repo_license: MIT (LICENSE file, 'Copyright (c) 2026 Ruiyi Wang'); README badge says Apache-2.0 - inconsistent

dependence.note: GPT-4 role-plays CBT patients from expert-authored cognitive models (PATIENT-PSI); the core outcomes are ratings by 20 mental-health experts and 13 trainees who interacted with the simulated patients. GPT-4 Turbo appears only in dataset construction (summaries of licensed therapy transcripts that inspired the cognitive models).

claim.statement: PATIENT-PSI (GPT-4 prompted with an expert-created CCD cognitive model plus a conversational-style instruction) is rated by 20 experts as significantly more realistic than a vanilla GPT-4 patient baseline (mean pairwise fidelity preference mu = 1.3 on a -2..2 scale, p < 1e-4; Table 3; per-dimension mu = 0.6/1.1/1.3 for maladaptive cognitions/emotional states/conversational styles) and as capturing its reference cognitive model with mean accuracy 4.0/5 overall (95% CI [3.7, 4.2]; Table 12), with 80-88% of simulated patients rated very-to-extremely accurate per component (Section 4.2).
claim.metric: expert pairwise comparison (-2..2) of fidelity vs baseline; 5-point Likert accuracy per CCD component; model-side proxy: GPT-4-as-judge accuracy/macro-F1 of PATIENT-PSI vs its reference cognitive model over the 40 expert conversations (Table 6)
claim.original_source: Tables 3, 6, 11, 12 and Sections 4.1-4.2, 5 of the EMNLP paper

protocol.model: 'gpt-4' alias (lib/chat/actions.tsx, Vercel AI SDK) for the simulated patient and the GPT-4 baseline; 'GPT-4 Turbo (OpenAI, 2023)' only for transcript summarisation during PATIENT-PSI-CM construction; judges: GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B at temperature 1.0
protocol.model_status: live model NOT an experimental arm: gpt-4-turbo was used only to summarise licensed transcripts (auxiliary data-construction step). The patient simulator ran on the 'gpt-4' alias (gpt-4-0613, dead) via the app; snapshot unpinned.
protocol.endpoint: chat completions through the Next.js/Vercel app (app/api, lib/chat/actions.tsx); python/generation/generate.py (langchain ChatOpenAI, GENERATOR_MODEL=gpt-4, temperature 1.0) for cognitive-model extraction
protocol.prompt_source: app/api/getDataFromKV.ts formatPromptString (patient system prompt), app/api/data/patient-types.jsx (six conversational-style instructions), python/generation/generation_template.py (CCD extraction prompt); Appendix C.3-C.4 of the paper

messages.content: Imagine you are {name}, a patient who has been experiencing mental health challenges. ... Patient History: {history} ... Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram: Core Beliefs / Intermediate Beliefs / ... Situation / Automatic Thoughts / Emotions / Behavior ... guidelines 1-5 (style instruction, natural language, gradual revelation, consistency, dynamic conversation) ... Limit each of your responses to a maximum of 5 sentences.

params.temperature: not set in the chat app (SDK default); 1.0 for CM generation and for the LLM judges

protocol.n_items: 66 cognitive models used in the user study; 33 participants x 2 sessions per system; 40 expert conversations for the automatic evaluation
protocol.evaluation: Core: human questionnaires (experts/trainees) - not re-measurable without new participants. Model-side: Table 6 LLM-judge accuracy needs the 40 archived conversations (de-identified, 'consented to be released for research purposes' but not in the repo) and the PATIENT-PSI-CM dataset (by request, institutions with an Alexander Street subscription).

artifacts.data_path: PATIENT-PSI-CM: request form https://forms.gle/pQ3g6YVFrEWjBU2H7 (restricted); example profiles in python/data/profiles.json (Beck Institute 'Abe' example); user-study conversations not released
artifacts.data_license: code MIT; dataset restricted to academic institutions with an Alexander Street subscription
artifacts.notes: Judge prompts and the automatic-evaluation scripts are not in the repository.

blockers: core outcomes are expert/trainee ratings from live sessions - only model outputs re-executable, and the patient simulation needs a human therapist interlocutor
live model not an experimental arm (GPT-4 Turbo only summarised transcripts); the simulator used the unpinned 'gpt-4' alias (gpt-4-0613, dead)
PATIENT-PSI-CM dataset and the 40 conversations are restricted/unreleased; judge prompts not released
source transcripts come from a licensed database (Alexander Street)

budget.assumptions: conditional model-side proxy only: re-run the LLM-judge accuracy (Table 6) with a live judge over 40 conversations x 8 components x 3 seeds, ~3,000 input tokens per call - requires the unreleased conversations and cognitive models. A new simulated-patient session set would additionally need human therapists.

judgment.rule: Not judgeable under ANALYSIS_PLAN section 1 for the core claim (human fidelity/accuracy ratings). If the proxy is approved: survival if judge-measured component accuracies stay >= 0.8 for text fields and macro-F1 for core beliefs/emotions stays within +/- 0.1 of 0.80/0.72; note that the judge itself changes model, confounding the comparison.
judgment.notes: The paper itself shows LLM judges disagree with experts (Figure 5), so a judge-based proxy is weak evidence for the human-rated claim.

user_checks: Should we request PATIENT-PSI-CM and the 40 de-identified expert conversations from the authors to enable the Table 6 proxy?
Record this paper as 'human-outcome; live model auxiliary only' - agree?
domain_notes: CBT cognitive models follow Beck's Cognitive Conceptualization Diagram (19 core-belief categories, 9 emotions); the fidelity construct is clinical realism judged by practising clinicians, which no automatic metric replaces. The paper reports that GPT-4 and Llama-3 judges systematically favour the vanilla GPT-4 baseline, i.e. LLM-as-judge is anti-correlated with expert judgment here - relevant for any judge-based successor comparison.
